overview: The Tree Depth First Search (DFS) pattern is a structural traversal framework that explores a tree data structure by diving as deep as possible down each branch vertically before backtracking. This approach naturally utilizes the runtime Call Stack (via recursion) or an explicit `std::stack` container to preserve parent state metrics during down-stream runs. By propagating state variables down parent-child link pathways, Tree DFS solves tracking validation, complete pathway generation, and structural node-to-node metrics in linear $O(N)$ time.
recognition_signals: Hierarchical Node Links: The data structure consists of branched node entities containing standard `left` and `right` child references.
Vertical Path Requirements: The problem requirements specifically target deep, continuous combinations (e.g., "root-to-leaf path," "continuous sequence," "ancestor-to-descendant lines").
Complete Path Generation: Building or returning an explicit list of all full sequence variations that fit a constraint.
Backtracking Operations: Requirements that mandate clearing or undoing structural path choices when a terminal leaf node fails a constraint.

Bottom-Up State Synthesis: Problems requiring child nodes to fully compute and return values up to their parent anchors before a final calculation can execute (e.g., computing tree diameters or maximum path sums).

mental_model.analogy: Imagine exploring a deep, unfamiliar maze or walking through an ancestral family history chart.
mental_model.description:
Imagine exploring a deep, unfamiliar maze or walking through an ancestral family history chart.

Instead of floating in a hot-air balloon to count house rooftops floor-by-floor from above, you enter the front door of the main estate (the root). You choose the leftmost corridor and walk down it continuously, ignoring side doors until you hit a dead-end wall (a leaf node). While walking, you note down every hallway turn onto a single tracing notepad. When you hit the dead-end, you evaluate your tracking page. To explore further, you take a single step back to the nearest junction, erase the last recorded dead-end from your notepad, and immediately explore the next unresolved side passage.

brute_force_journey.brute_force_description: An unoptimized approach to path evaluation copies the cumulative tracing list entirely at every level jump, or runs a fresh, un-cached top-down verification check from every internal node.
brute_force_journey.inefficiency_observation: Overlapping subsegments perform duplicate evaluations of identical elements.
brute_force_journey.optimization_concept:
```
  Brute Force
  [Duplicate and pass full path vectors by value down recursive calls -> High Memory Overhead]
       ↓
  Observation
  [A single path can be shared globally across calls if we remove the current node when returning]
       ↓
  Optimization
  [Pass a single path vector by reference, and execute an explicit vector.pop_back() to backtrack]
       ↓
  Final Pattern
  [Perform in-place path mutations on a single forward pass -> O(N) Time, O(H) Space]

```

---

animation_steps.description: Traverse to root node 1. Push to path stack: [1].
Traverse down left branch to node 2. Stack path: [1, 2]. Leaf reached, backtrack.
Traverse down right branch to node 3. Stack path: [1, 3]. Traversal finished.

variants.name: **Top-Down Decision**
variants.description: Root $\rightarrow$ Leaf (Subtract current node value from target parameter.)

variants.name: **Path Generation**
variants.description: Reference Pass (Push node to path vector, drill down, then execute an explicit pop step to backtrack.)

variants.name: **Numeric Accumulation**
variants.description: Scalar Shifting (Compute values across rows using positional multiplication: `sum = sum * 10 + val`.)

variants.name: **Bottom-Up Merge**
variants.description: Leaf $\rightarrow$ Root (Fetch values from children first, then compute localized results at the parent.)

common_mistakes.description: **Missing Backtracking Pop steps:** Forgetting to call `path.pop_back()` before a recursive helper function exits. This leaves elements from a completed branch inside the global reference vector, corrupting subsequent path calculations.

**Early Null Pointer Processing Errors:** Writing validation checks like `if (!node) return (sum == 0);`. If an internal node has only a single child, this check will process the empty branch as a valid path, incorrectly triggering a leaf node status. Always verify leaf nodes using explicit child null tests: `if (!node->left && !node->right)`.

**Disrupting Short-Circuit Logic:** Mixing up logical short-circuit behaviors (`||` vs `&&`). For example, in path matching tasks, writing checks that force full execution down both branches when a single valid path is already confirmed.

**Ignoring Negative Node Contributions:** Short-circuiting or cutting loops short when a running sum exceeds a target value, assuming it can no longer match. If the tree contains negative node values, a sum that is currently too large can drop back down to match the target exactly later.

cheat_sheet: When writing bottom-up structural algorithms like Tree Diameter or Maximum Path Sum, think of it as a corporate chain of command:
A parent node cannot compute its own maximum path value until its left and right child managers complete their independent investigations and report back.
1. Execute the recursive calls first to let the child nodes compute their results.
2. Once they return their values, calculate the localized maximum at the parent node (`left + right + node->val`).
4. Finally, hand back only the single strongest branch up to your supervisor node: `return max(left, right) + node->val`.
